slides.title: Why multiple heads?
slides.body:
Single-head attention is one weighted average per token. That's expressive — but every token's output is computed the *same way*. If you want a model that can both track syntax (where attention should be local) and resolve coreference (where attention reaches far back), one attention pattern isn't enough.

**Multi-head attention** runs `h` independent attention computations in parallel. Each head has its own learned projections of Q, K, V, so each head can specialize. One head might learn locality. Another might learn pronoun resolution. A third might learn induction (copy the next token after a previous occurrence).

At the end, the head outputs are concatenated and projected back to `d_model`.

slides.title: The shapes
slides.body:
Each head projects from the full `d_model` down to `d_k = d_model / h`. So if `d_model = 512` and `h = 8`, every head sees 64-dimensional Q, K, V.

```
input X: [batch, seq_len, d_model]
  ↓ W_Q^h, W_K^h, W_V^h  (one set per head h)
Q_h, K_h, V_h: [batch, seq_len, d_k]
  ↓ scaled-dot-product-attention
head_h: [batch, seq_len, d_k]
  ↓ concat across all h heads
concat: [batch, seq_len, h * d_k = d_model]
  ↓ W_O
output: [batch, seq_len, d_model]
```

The **output projection** `W_O` is critical. Without it, the heads' outputs would just sit side-by-side; `W_O` lets the model **mix** information from different heads into a single representation.

Notice the parameter count is the same as one big `d_model × d_model` attention — multi-head doesn't add capacity, it adds **diversity** of attention patterns at the same capacity.

question.question: If you set n_heads=1 with the same total d_model, what changes vs an h=8 multi-head model?
options: Nothing — multi-head is just an optimization for parallelism
The model can only learn ONE attention pattern per layer; with h=8 it could learn up to 8 different patterns at the same capacity
Single-head is strictly better because there's no head-output concatenation
question.explanation: Multi-head's value is diversity, not capacity. Same total parameter count (one big attention vs h smaller ones); but multi-head can learn 8 different attention patterns at once, while single-head has to compress everything into one. This is why dropping to h=1 typically hurts language modeling significantly.

slides.title: What the heads actually learn
slides.body:
Empirical results from BERT and GPT-2 analyses:

- **Previous-token heads** (attention diagonal shifted by one) — copy what was just said.
- **Locality heads** — soft attention to a nearby window. Useful for syntax.
- **Punctuation heads** — heavily attend to commas, periods, end-of-sentence markers. Helps with phrase boundaries.
- **Coreference heads** — the pronoun-resolution example we saw earlier.
- **Induction heads** (Olsson et al. 2022) — composed across layers: layer L has a previous-token head; layer L+1 attends back to find the matching token, then 'reads' the next token after it. This is how `"A B ... A → B"` works.

Not every head specializes cleanly. Many heads have diffuse, hard-to-interpret patterns. The **superposition** hypothesis says heads pack multiple weak features into the same parameters — that's why mech-interp work has moved toward sparse autoencoders for cleaner features.

slides.title: Grouped-query attention
slides.body:
At inference time, multi-head attention dominates memory bandwidth: every head needs its own K and V cached for every token in the context. With `h=32` heads and a long context, this is a lot.

**Grouped-query attention (GQA)** saves bandwidth by sharing K and V across groups of heads. With `h=32` query heads and `g=8` KV groups, each KV head is shared by 4 query heads. Memory drops 4×; quality is mostly preserved.

**Multi-query attention (MQA)** is the extreme: all heads share a single K and V. Even more savings but more quality loss.

LLaMA-2 70B uses GQA with 8 KV heads (down from 64 in standard MHA). Mistral 7B does the same. This is the most common architectural variation you'll see in modern open models — at no quality cost worth measuring on the standard evals.

question.question: Why does grouped-query attention (GQA) reduce inference memory but keep training the same?
options: GQA only applies during inference; at training it falls back to standard MHA
GQA shares K and V across head groups, so the KV-cache (built only at inference) is smaller; the forward-pass FLOPs are similar
question.explanation: GQA's win is in the KV-cache — the per-token K and V tensors that get stored for the entire context during autoregressive generation. With fewer KV groups, the cache is proportionally smaller. The training-time forward + backward work is dominated by FLOPs, which barely change.

slides.title: What's next
slides.body:
Multi-head attention is the workhorse of every transformer block. Each attention sublayer is followed by a position-wise [[feed-forward-networks]] (FFN), and both wrap in [[residual-connections]] + layer norm to make the deep stack trainable.

After this lesson you should be able to:
- Compute the parameter count of a multi-head attention layer
- Explain why multi-head adds diversity, not capacity
- Describe one head specialization pattern (induction, locality, etc.)
- Recognize GQA in a model card and know what tradeoff it implies

The FFN is up next — it's the part of the transformer that actually does most of the parameter math.
